paras: The Orchard Park dynamiting was an attack early on August 8, 1903, in which a mob of "men and boys" dynamited and set fire to a house being built for a Black woman named Warner in Orchard Park, a suburb of Oklahoma City, Oklahoma Territory. It followed orders from armed, masked white men that the suburb's Black residents leave, and their refusal and arming led papers across the country to warn of a "race war." Black residents published an appeal for protection, and the Black press condemned the attack.

Orchard Park was a residence suburb of Oklahoma City in which Black families owned homes. According to the Oklahoman, as copied by the Wichita Daily Eagle, armed and masked men called at a house occupied by Black residents after midnight in the last days of July and gave them twenty-four hours to leave what they called "a white man's residence district." A deputy sheriff and a policeman who approached the party faced "a dozen winchesters," were ordered to "git," and withdrew without arrests.
The spokesman warned that "if you do not pack up and get out of here you will regret it," but the two Black families in the house did not move, and Black homeowners in the suburb armed themselves.

Early on Saturday, August 8, according to an Oklahoma City dispatch to the Dallas News, a mob of men and boys dynamited and set fire to the house being built for "a negro woman named Warner." The house was "badly wrecked," and the explosion shook that part of the city. The Daily Ardmoreite named the owner "Mrs. Warner" and linked the attack to the masked mob's visit "a few nights ago."

The dispatch said the Black residents, warned to leave, had refused and would protect their property "at the risk of their lives," some stocking their homes with arms "until they look like arsenals." None of the reports mentions anyone killed or injured.

On August 13 an Oklahoma City dispatch said Black residents had appealed to the public and police for protection from "dynamiters who have operated in Orchard park," and that authorities would use "summary measures" if necessary. The appeal said a Black resident had recently bought property in Orchard Park from a white seller who encouraged the purchase, and that one citizen's property had been dynamited only because "they are simply negroes." Thirteen men signed it, among them J. Aarvin Byrd, R. B. Williams and F. G. Houston.
No report of arrests, an inquest or a prosecution was found in the coverage.

The Dallas News dispatch ran widely on August 9 and 10 under headlines stressing racial conflict, such as "Race Trouble Is Threatened" (Montgomery Advertiser), "Do Not Like the Negroes" (Birmingham Age-Herald) and "Race War Feared" (Indianapolis Journal). The Louisville Courier-Journal led with "Negroes Arm and Prepare To Defend Themselves," while the Atlanta Constitution named the attackers: "Whites Dynamite Negro House."

Weeklies cut the story to one-line items into late August, printing "Archard Park" or "Oklahouma Territory," and the Yorkville Enquirer added a line absent from the wire: "The whites say no Negro shall own property in the city."

The Western World, a Black weekly in Oklahoma City, wrote that "a few white ruffians" had tried to dynamite "a respected colored man's home" and blamed "the poor ignorant class of whites who are opposed to the prosperity of the colored people." It said white people had denounced the act, and its local column added, "Beans are still in the pot out in Orchard Park." The St. Paul Appeal remarked that the "superior" residents of Orchard Park "have shown their chivalry" by dynamiting a house being built by "an Afro-American woman."
Where white wire reports centered on Black residents arming and a coming race war, the Black press and the residents' appeal treated the attack as lawlessness against Black property owners.

The same-day Dallas News dispatch dated the attack early August 8, but the Keowee Courier and Anderson Intelligencer said Thursday, the Yorkville Enquirer "last Saturday," and the Daily Ardmoreite, under an August 10 dateline, "last night." The wire said the woman's house was "badly wrecked"; the Western World said white men "tried to dynamite" a "colored man's home."

reader.title: Orchard Park dynamiting
bases: A mob dynamited and set fire to a house being built for a Black woman (A5, A11, A13), part of a campaign by whites to drive Black residents out of the suburb (A1, A3).

The Dallas News wire (A5), the Oklahoma Daily Ardmoreite (A13), the Oklahoma City Black weekly (A21) and the residents' appeal (A24) independently report the dynamiting, though they differ on date and damage.

accounts.label: Dallas News wire
accounts.gist: A mob of men and boys dynamited and burned a house being built for a Black woman named Warner; Black residents warned to leave refused and armed themselves; a race war was feared.

accounts.label: Oklahoman (via Wichita Daily Eagle)
accounts.gist: Days earlier a masked, armed party ordered Black residents out of Orchard Park within 24 hours as 'a white man's residence district' and drove off a deputy and a policeman at rifle point.

accounts.label: Black correspondent (Western World)
accounts.gist: A few white ruffians tried to dynamite a respected colored man's home; poor whites opposed to Black prosperity were responsible, and white people denounced the act.

accounts.label: Black residents' appeal
accounts.gist: A Black citizen bought property from a white seller; the property was dynamited only because the owners were Black; the signers asked white citizens and police for protection.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'Race War Feared', 'Do Not Like the Negroes' and 'Negroes Arm and Prepare To Defend Themselves' foreground Black arming and a coming race war.
Atlanta Constitution names the attackers in its headline, 'Whites Dynamite Negro House'.
Wichita Daily Eagle printed the Black residents' appeal in full under 'Negroes Make Appeal'.
Western World: 'white ruffians', 'poor ignorant class of whites who are opposed to the prosperity of the colored people'.
St. Paul Appeal: the 'superior' residents 'have shown their chivalry' by dynamiting an Afro-American woman's house.

conflicts.note: The same-day Dallas News dispatch is the earliest and most direct; the rest are later rewrites.
